RNA polymerase. The enzyme that catalyzes transcription—the synthesis of RNA from a DNA template strand in the five-prime to three-prime direction. Unlike DNA polymerase, it requires no primer, initiates synthesis directly without any starter segment, and uses ribonucleotides instead of deoxyribonucleotides. The enzyme recognizes promoter sequences to start transcription and continues until termination signals halt synthesis. RNA polymerase catalyzes the formation of phosphodiester bonds between ribonucleotide triphosphates. It reads the DNA template in the three-prime to five-prime direction while synthesizing RNA in the five-prime to three-prime direction. Unlike DNA polymerase, no primer is needed—this is a major difference. The enzyme initiates transcription directly. In prokaryotes, a single RNA polymerase catalyzes all transcription. In eukaryotes, three main polymerases exist: Pol I synthesizes ribosomal RNA, Pol II synthesizes messenger RNA, and Pol III synthesizes transfer RNA. Each recognizes different promoter elements. In E. coli, promoters contain minus-ten and minus-thirty boxes where RNA polymerase recognizes and unwinds DNA. Eukaryotic promoters contain a T-A-T-A box. Transcription terminates through intrinsic mechanisms involving hairpin structures or through rho protein-dependent mechanisms in prokaryotes, while in eukaryotes polyadenylation signals direct the process. Transcription is the first step of gene expression—converting genetic instructions into functional RNA molecules. RNA polymerase is the molecular reader that makes this conversion possible. Unlike replication, which copies the entire genome with nearly perfect fidelity, transcription is selective and regulated. Cells turn genes on and off through RNA polymerase binding and activity.
